paragraphs: When the people in charge can’t agree, things start to pause
First, What Does the Government Do?

The U.S. government provides important services that keep the country running, like defending the nation, building roads, supporting healthcare, and funding schools. It also helps people through programs like Social Security, food assistance, and disaster relief.
To keep all this going, the government needs money, and that money comes from something called a federal budget.
What Is a Government Shutdown?
A government shutdown happens when Congress can’t agree on a new budget before a deadline.
That means the government doesn’t have permission to spend money, so many services must pause or shut down.
Why Can’t They Just Agree?

U.S. Congress is made up of two groups: the House of Representatives and the Senate. They have to vote to approve the budget, and if they (usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers) disagree about how to spend the money, the government can’t move forward.
Sometimes they disagree on:
How much to spend on defense or schools
Whether to cut or increase certain programs
Tax changes or debt limits
If no agreement is reached by the deadline, shutdown happens.
What Happens During a Shutdown?
When the government shuts down, some things stop and some keep going. Some workers still have to work but don’t get paid until later. This can be really hard for families who depend on those jobs.
Stays Open:
Military and national security (but workers may not be paid right away)
Air traffic control and mail delivery
Social Security and Medicare payments (they’re mandatory programs)
Gets Paused:
National parks and museums may close
NASA, science labs, and safety inspections may pause
Many government workers are sent home without pay. This is called being “furloughed”

Because Social Security and Medicare become illegal

questions.question: According to "Why Can’t They Just Agree?", what two groups make up U.S. Congress and must vote to approve the budget?

Military leaders and mail carriers
The House of Representatives and the Senate
Social Security and Medicare

Option C is correct (O): Section 3 states directly: "U.S. Congress is made up of two groups: the House of Representatives and the Senate. They have to vote to approve the budget..."
Option A is incorrect (X): Parks and safety inspections are services that may pause during a shutdown.
Option B is incorrect (X): Military and mail delivery are listed under "Stays Open:", not as parts of Congress.
Option D is incorrect (X): Social Security and Medicare are mandatory programs, not legislative chambers.

questions.question: According to "Why Can’t They Just Agree?", which topics do lawmakers sometimes disagree on, and what happens if no agreement is reached by the deadline?
options: They disagree on weather forecasts and museum tickets, and Congress shuts down permanently.
They disagree on how much to spend on defense or schools, whether to cut or increase certain programs, or tax changes or debt limits; if no agreement is reached by the deadline, shutdown happens.
They disagree on air traffic routes and mail schedules, and Medicare is immediately canceled.
They disagree only on NASA funding, and the House of Representatives approves the budget alone without a vote.
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct (O): Section 3 lists all three disagreement points ("How much to spend on defense or schools", "Whether to cut or increase certain programs", "Tax changes or debt limits") and concludes: "If no agreement is reached by the deadline, shutdown happens."
Option A is incorrect (X): Weather forecasts and museum tickets are not in the list, and a shutdown pauses services rather than ending Congress permanently.
Option C is incorrect (X): Air traffic control, mail delivery, and Medicare stay open.
Option D is incorrect (X): Both groups in Congress have to vote to approve the budget.

questions.question: According to "What Happens During a Shutdown?", which pair accurately contrasts something that stays open with something that gets paused?
options: National parks stay open, while mail delivery gets paused.
NASA and science labs stay open, while Social Security payments get paused.
Air traffic control and Medicare payments stay open, while national parks and safety inspections may close or pause.
Museums stay open, while military and national security get paused.
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct (O): Under "Stays Open:", the article lists military and national security, air traffic control and mail delivery, and Social Security and Medicare payments. Under "Gets Paused:", it lists national parks and museums, NASA, science labs, and safety inspections.
Option A is incorrect (X): It reverses both—national parks may close, while mail delivery stays open.
Option B is incorrect (X): NASA and science labs may pause, while Social Security stays open.
Option D is incorrect (X): Museums may close, while military and national security stay open.

questions.question: According to "What Happens During a Shutdown?", how can a shutdown affect government workers and their pay?
options: All government workers stop working and receive double pay right away.
Some workers still have to work without getting paid until later, while many other workers are sent home without pay (called being "furloughed").
Military workers are sent home first, while museum workers receive immediate mandatory payments.
Only families without government jobs are affected, because all workers are paid on time.
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct (O): Section 4 explains that "Some workers still have to work but don’t get paid until later" (including military and national security workers who "may not be paid right away"), and under "Gets Paused:", "Many government workers are sent home without pay. This is called being “furloughed”".
Option A is incorrect (X): Some workers must still work, and neither group gets paid right away.
Option C is incorrect (X): Military and national security stay open (though workers may not be paid right away), while museums may close.
Option D is incorrect (X): The text specifically notes this can be really hard for families who depend on those jobs.

languageFocus.title: Language Focus
languageFocus.instructions: Study these seven civic writing and grammar patterns from the article. Apply them in Writing Practice and the final Writing Task.
languageFocus.topic: Cause/Effect, When-Clauses, Modals, Passive Voice, Contrast, Lists & Civic Vocabulary
languageFocus.explanation: Clear civic explanation connects causes to outcomes, uses accurate modals and passive verbs, contrasts open vs. paused services, organizes examples cleanly in lists, and uses exact civic vocabulary with source attribution.

patterns.name: 1. Cause and Effect Language
patterns.explanation: Connect reasons and results clearly using when, that means, so, because, as a result, and if.
patterns.example: Congress missed the deadline; as a result, the government lost permission to spend money, so many services paused.
patterns.sourceExample: That means the government doesn’t have permission to spend money, so many services must pause or shut down.

patterns.name: 2. When-Clauses (Time & General Condition)
patterns.explanation: Use When + present simple to explain what regularly happens whenever a civic event occurs.
patterns.example: When lawmakers disagree on the federal budget, the government cannot move forward.
patterns.sourceExample: A government shutdown happens when Congress can’t agree on a new budget before a deadline. / When the government shuts down, some things stop and some keep going.

patterns.name: 3. Modals (can’t, must, may, have to)
patterns.explanation: Choose modals carefully to match exact meaning: can’t (inability to agree/move forward), have to / must (legal requirement), and may (possibility, not certainty).
patterns.example: Lawmakers have to vote on the budget; without permission, services must pause and parks may close.
patterns.sourceExample: They have to vote to approve the budget... so many services must pause or shut down... National parks and museums may close.

patterns.name: 4. Passive Voice (is made up of, is reached, be paid, are sent, is called)
patterns.explanation: Use be + past participle when the institution, agreement, or workers receive the action rather than naming who performs it.
patterns.example: If no agreement is reached, many workers are sent home without pay and may not be paid right away.
patterns.sourceExample: U.S. Congress is made up of two groups... If no agreement is reached... workers may not be paid right away... Many government workers are sent home without pay. This is called being “furloughed”

patterns.name: 5. Contrast Structures
patterns.explanation: Contrast open vs. paused services and opposing choices using but, however, while, some... and some..., and whether... or...
patterns.example: Some programs stay open, whereas national parks may close; meanwhile, some workers keep working while others are furloughed.
patterns.sourceExample: When the government shuts down, some things stop and some keep going. Some workers still have to work but don’t get paid until later.

patterns.name: 6. Lists & Parallel Series
patterns.explanation: Group three or more related civic services or disagreement points in parallel grammatical forms (all -ing phrases, all nouns, or balanced bullet phrases).
patterns.example: The budget supports defending the nation, building roads, supporting healthcare, and funding schools.
patterns.sourceExample: like defending the nation, building roads, supporting healthcare, and funding schools... Social Security, food assistance, and disaster relief.

patterns.name: 7. Civic Vocabulary & Source Attribution
patterns.explanation: Use exact civic terms (federal budget, Congress, House of Representatives, Senate, lawmakers, mandatory, furloughed) and anchor claims with "According to the article,".
patterns.example: According to the article, mandatory programs such as Social Security and Medicare continue during a shutdown.
patterns.sourceExample: Social Security and Medicare payments (they’re mandatory programs) / This is called being “furloughed”

Meanwhile, some workers still have to work without getting paid right away, while many workers are sent home without pay—called being "furloughed"—which can be "really hard for families who depend on those jobs."

languageFocus: Cause/effect: when Congress can’t agree...; That means...; so many services must pause; If no agreement is reached...; because (in student writing).
When-clauses: When the people in charge can’t agree...; when Congress can’t agree...; When the government shuts down...
Modals: can’t (inability), doesn’t have / have to (requirement), must (necessity), may / may not (possibility).
Passive voice: is made up of, is reached, not be paid, are sent home, is called.
Contrast: Whether to cut or increase...; some things stop and some keep going; still have to work but don’t get paid until later; Stays Open vs. Gets Paused.

Lists: defending the nation, building roads, supporting healthcare, and funding schools; Social Security, food assistance, and disaster relief; 3 disagreement bullets; 3 Stays Open bullets; 3 Gets Paused bullets.
Civic vocabulary: federal budget, service, deadline, permission, Congress, lawmakers, defense, mandatory, furloughed, disaster relief.

writingPractice.wp1: A government shutdown happens when Congress cannot agree on a new federal budget before a deadline. Because the government does not have permission to spend money, many services must pause or shut down.
writingPractice.wp2: U.S. Congress is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate, and lawmakers may disagree on defense or school spending, cutting or increasing programs, or tax changes and debt limits. If no agreement is reached by the deadline, shutdown happens.
writingPractice.wp3: During a shutdown, military and national security, air traffic control, mail delivery, and mandatory Social Security and Medicare payments stay open. However, national parks and museums may close, and NASA, science labs, and safety inspections may pause.
writingPractice.wp4: During a shutdown, some workers still have to work without getting paid right away, while many government workers are sent home without pay, which is called being furloughed. This is hard for families because they depend on those jobs.

answerKey.writingTask: Must be 100–140 words answering "According to the article, what is a government shutdown, why does it happen, and what happens to services and workers during it?" with source attribution, 3+ article details, cause/effect, open-vs-paused comparison, and worker/furlough impact.

teacher.modelAnswer: According to the article, a government shutdown happens when Congress cannot agree on a new federal budget before a deadline. Because lawmakers in the House of Representatives and the Senate disagree about spending on defense or schools, programs, taxes, or debt limits, the government loses permission to spend money, so many services must pause. During a shutdown, mandatory programs like Social Security and Medicare payments, along with military and national security, air traffic control, and mail delivery, stay open. However, national parks, museums, NASA, science labs, and safety inspections may close or pause. Overall, a shutdown creates hardship for families because some workers still work without immediate pay while many others are furloughed, or sent home without pay.

rubric.description: Defines a government shutdown, explains why it happens, and explains effects on both services and workers.
rubric.excellent: Fully answers all three parts of the prompt: defines shutdown (missed budget deadline / no spending permission), explains Congress disagreement causes, and explains both service effects and worker/family impacts.
rubric.developing: Addresses most parts of the prompt but leaves out either why the shutdown occurs (permission/deadline) or one side of the service/worker effects.
rubric.beginning: Gives only a general or incomplete summary, missing the budget-deadline cause or how services and workers are affected.

rubric.description: Uses at least 3 accurate details from the article with clear attribution and zero outside facts.
rubric.excellent: Uses explicit attribution ("According to the article,") and 3+ specific source details (e.g., House and Senate, disagreement items, mandatory programs, specific open/paused services, furloughed workers) with no outside claims.
rubric.developing: Includes 1–2 specific details from the article or weak attribution; minor vagueness in service or worker examples.
rubric.beginning: Relies on vague general claims or introduces outside political facts not stated in the article.

rubric.description: Applies cause/effect, when/if clauses, modals, passive voice, contrast, lists, and civic vocabulary.
rubric.excellent: Effectively combines cause/effect connectors, when/if clauses, accurate modals (must/may), passive forms (are sent home / are furloughed), contrast markers (however, while), and civic vocabulary.
rubric.developing: Uses one or two target structures accurately, but repeats simple sentences or omits contrast or passive forms.
rubric.beginning: Shows minimal use of cause/effect, contrast, modals, or target civic vocabulary.

rubric.description: Follows a clear explanatory flow from definition and cause to open/paused effects and conclusion.
rubric.excellent: Clear topic sentence with attribution, logical cause-to-effect middle comparing services and workers, smooth transitions, and a clear concluding sentence.
rubric.developing: Generally clear sequence, though transitions between causes and effects or the concluding sentence feel abrupt.
rubric.beginning: Ideas appear disconnected or lack a clear topic sentence and concluding wrap-up.

rubric.description: Grammar, spelling, capitalization of proper nouns, punctuation, and 100–140 word count target.
rubric.excellent: Strictly 100–140 words; accurate subject-verb agreement, passive participles, capitalization (U.S. Congress, House of Representatives, Senate, Social Security, Medicare, NASA), and punctuation.
rubric.developing: Minor grammar, article, or capitalization slips that do not obscure meaning, or word count slightly outside 100–140.
rubric.beginning: Frequent grammar or mechanics errors that interfere with meaning, or far below 100 words.

teacherNotes.topic: Core Civics Concept: Services Need Budget Money
teacherNotes.note: Teach strictly from Section 1: government services (defending the nation, roads, healthcare, schools) and programs (Social Security, food assistance, disaster relief) need money from a federal budget to keep running.

Teach strictly from Sections 2 and 3: U.S. Congress (the House of Representatives and the Senate) must vote to approve the budget. If lawmakers (usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers) disagree on defense/school spending, cutting/increasing programs, or tax changes/debt limits and no agreement is reached by the deadline, the government loses permission to spend money and shutdown happens.

teacherNotes.topic: Open vs. Paused Services & Worker Impacts
teacherNotes.note: Teach strictly from Section 4: some things stay open (military and national security, air traffic control and mail delivery, and mandatory Social Security and Medicare payments) while others may close or pause (national parks and museums, NASA, science labs, safety inspections). Workers are affected in two ways: some must still work without getting paid right away/until later, while many are sent home without pay (being "furloughed"), creating hardship for families.

teacherNotes.topic: Strict Neutrality — No Political Claims or Outside Facts
teacherNotes.note: Make NO political claims and NO party judgments about Democrats or Republicans. Do not introduce outside details (such as specific U.S. fiscal dates, named politicians, past shutdown years, or laws not named in the article). Keep all teaching anchored to the canonical 3-image source.

teachingScript.objective: Introduce the civics topic, 3-image source structure, and source-strict rule.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Greet students, display the title, subtitle, and unit goal, and explain that all answers must stay strictly inside the supplied article without outside politics.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Good morning, everyone! / Today we are reading / a Grade 9 civics article: / "What Happens When a Government Shuts Down?" / Notice the subtitle: / "When the people in charge can’t agree, / things start to pause." / Keep one rule in mind: / we use only the facts / written in our three-part article.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 안녕하세요 여러분! 오늘 우리는 9학년 시민(Civics) 읽기 지문 "What Happens When a Government Shuts Down?"을 함께 읽습니다. 부제목 "책임자들이 합의하지 못하면 일들이 멈추기 시작한다"를 보세요. 오늘의 핵심 규칙은 외부 배경지식이나 정치적 판단을 넣지 않고 반드시 세 이미지로 구성된 본문 안의 사실만 사용하는 것입니다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students read the lesson header, title, subtitle, and goal, noting the source-only rule (G1: underline key nouns in the title; G2: predict the cause-and-effect link in the subtitle).
teachingScript.misconception: Assuming a government shutdown means the entire government disappears or stops every service completely.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Point to the word "pause" in the subtitle and clarify that we will check which things stay open and which things pause (G1: highlight "pause"; G2: contrast "pause" with "shut down").
teachingScript.transition: Before reading the article, let us activate our ideas with three quick warm-up questions.

teachingScript.objective: Build readiness around public services, budget disagreement before deadlines, and essential vs. non-essential pausing.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Guide pairs through Warm-up Q1–Q3 using the sentence starters and elicit brief oral/written responses.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Look at Question 1: / What services does a government provide / every day? / Next, Question 2: / Why might leaders disagree / on how to spend money / before a deadline? / Finally, Question 3: / If spending pauses, / what should stay open / and what might pause?
teachingScript.scriptKo: 1번 질문을 봅시다. 정부는 매일 어떤 서비스를 제공할까요? 다음으로 2번: 지도자들은 왜 마감 시한 전에 돈 쓰는 방법에 대해 의견이 다를 수 있을까요? 마지막 3번: 지출이 멈춘다면 무엇이 계속 열려 있어야 하고 무엇이 잠시 멈출 수 있을까요?
teachingScript.studentActions: Students discuss in pairs and draft 1–2 sentence responses (G1: complete the sentence starters; G2: give two concrete examples per question).
teachingScript.misconception: Blaming one political side or guessing unrelated economic crises before reading.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Keep discussion neutral and focused on how budgets require agreement on priorities (G1: use "disagree on how to spend money"; G2: connect disagreement to missing a deadline).
teachingScript.transition: Now let us read the exact three-page article carefully to verify how a shutdown really works.

teachingScript.objective: Read all 4 sections across the 3 ordered source pages with chunking, preserving exact wording and bullet boundaries.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Read Pages 1, 2, and 3 aloud with chunk pauses; highlight the 4 question headings, 3 lead-in colons, and 9 bullets.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Follow along across our three source pages. / Page 1 asks two questions: / What does the government do, / and what is a shutdown? / Page 2 asks: / Why can’t they just agree? / Watch the three disagreement bullets / and the deadline sentence. / Page 3 compares two lists: / "Stays Open:" versus "Gets Paused:" / and shows how workers are affected.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 세 쪽으로 구성된 원문 자료를 함께 따라 읽겠습니다. 1쪽에서는 두 가지 질문, 즉 정부가 하는 일과 셧다운이 무엇인지 묻습니다. 2쪽에서는 왜 합의하지 못하는지 물으며 3개의 불일치 항목과 마감 시한 문장을 다룹니다. 3쪽에서는 "계속 운영되는 분야:"와 "일시 중단되는 분야:" 두 목록을 대조하며 근로자들에게 미치는 영향을 보여 줍니다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students track the 4 headings and circle cause words (when, so, if) and contrast pairs (G1: color-code Stays Open vs. Gets Paused; G2: annotate modal verbs and parentheses).
teachingScript.misconception: Thinking workers who stay on the job get paid normally right away, or confusing "mandatory" with optional.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Direct attention to "(but workers may not be paid right away)" and "(they’re mandatory programs)" inside the Stays Open bullets (G1: match parentheses to the main bullet; G2: explain why mandatory matters).
teachingScript.transition: Next, let us examine the 10 key civic vocabulary terms in context.

teachingScript.objective: Master all 10 target vocabulary items with English definitions, Korean meanings, and exact source examples.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Review pronunciation, parts of speech, and source sentences for all 10 terms from "federal budget" to "disaster relief".
teachingScript.scriptEn: Check all ten vocabulary cards. / Connect "federal budget," / "deadline," and "permission": / without budget agreement before a deadline, / there is no permission to spend. / Next, pair "Congress" and "lawmakers," / then compare "mandatory" / with being "furloughed."
teachingScript.scriptKo: 열 개의 어휘 카드를 확인합시다. "federal budget(연방 예산)", "deadline(마감 시한)", "permission(허가)"을 연결해 보세요. 마감 시한 전에 예산 합의가 없으면 지출 허가가 사라집니다. 이어서 "Congress(의회)"와 "lawmakers(의원들)"를 짝짓고, "mandatory(의무적인)"와 "furloughed(무급 일시 휴직된)"를 비교해 봅시다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students pronounce each term, check Korean meanings, and underline where each appears in the article (G1: match Korean meaning to source sentence; G2: explain how "mandatory" differs from "furloughed").
teachingScript.misconception: Confusing "furloughed" (sent home without pay) with working without immediate pay, or thinking "Congress" means only the President.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Point back to Section 3 ("House of Representatives and the Senate") and Section 4 ("sent home without pay. This is called being “furloughed”").
teachingScript.transition: Now let us check our understanding with Main Idea, Comprehension, and Evidence from the Text.

teachingScript.objective: Complete 1 Main Idea MCQ, 6 Reading Comprehension MCQs, and 3 Evidence written responses using Check & Compare.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Have students complete the 7 MCQs independently, verify section references, then write ev1–ev3 and test each with Check & Compare.
teachingScript.scriptEn: First, answer the Main Idea question / and all six Reading Comprehension questions. / Point to the exact heading / for every answer. / Then write your three Evidence answers / about the budget, / Congress disagreement, / and open versus paused services and workers. / Click Check & Compare / to inspect your quotes and model answers.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 먼저 Main Idea 문제와 6개의 Reading Comprehension 문제를 푸세요. 모든 문제마다 정확한 소제목 근거를 짚어 보세요. 그런 다음 예산, 의회 불일치, 그리고 계속/중단 서비스 및 근로자에 대한 3개의 Evidence 문항을 작성하고 Check & Compare를 눌러 인용과 모범 답안을 확인하세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students answer Main Idea + rc1–rc6, draft ev1–ev3, and run Check & Compare (G1: quote key phrases directly; G2: integrate source phrases smoothly into complete sentences).
teachingScript.misconception: Mixing up Stays Open items (parks vs. mail delivery) or skipping the worker/family impact in ev3.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Have students verify every ev3 claim against the two lists in Page 3 (G1: include at least 2 open + 2 paused examples; G2: distinguish delayed-pay workers from furloughed workers).
teachingScript.transition: With the source evidence solid, let us practice the 7 Language Focus patterns.

teachingScript.objective: Analyze all 7 target language patterns and complete Writing Practice wp1–wp4 with Check & Compare.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Model cause/effect, when/if clauses, modals, passive voice, contrast, lists, and civic vocabulary, then supervise wp1–wp4.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Look at the seven tools in Language Focus: / cause and effect, / when-clauses, / modals like "must" and "may," / passive verbs like "are sent home," / contrast words, / parallel lists, / and civic vocabulary. / Now write Practice items 1 to 4 / and test each one with Check & Compare.
teachingScript.scriptKo: Language Focus의 일곱 가지 도구를 보세요. 인과 표현, when절, "must"와 "may" 같은 조동사, "are sent home" 같은 수동태, 대조 표현, 나열 병렬 구조, 그리고 시민 어휘입니다. 이제 Writing Practice 1~4번을 작성하고 각각 Check & Compare로 점검하세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students write wp1 (cause), wp2 (deadline), wp3 (comparison), and wp4 (furlough/passive) and review feedback (G1: check capital letters, punctuation, and 1 vocab word; G2: combine when/if clauses with passive voice).
teachingScript.misconception: Writing active verbs instead of passive voice in wp4 (e.g., "workers furloughed" instead of "workers are furloughed / are sent home") or overstating "may close" as "always close."
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Coach "be + past participle" ("are sent home", "are furloughed") and remind students to use "may" for parks/museums/NASA (G1: use sentence frames; G2: refine modal precision).
teachingScript.transition: You now have all the evidence and sentence patterns ready for the 100–140 word Writing Task.

teachingScript.objective: Draft, check, and revise a 100–140 word paragraph answering the exact shutdown prompt with attribution and zero outside facts.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Review the prompt, 5-item checklist, and 100–140 word target; circulate while students run Check & Compare and revise.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Now write your main paragraph: / "According to the article, / what is a government shutdown, / why does it happen, / and what happens to services and workers during it?" / Aim for 100 to 140 words. / Include attribution, / three source details, / cause and effect, / and comparison. / Click Check & Compare, / compare with the model, / and revise.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 이제 핵심 쓰기 과제입니다. "According to the article, what is a government shutdown, why does it happen, and what happens to services and workers during it?"에 대해 100~140단어로 작성하세요. 출처 밝히기, 본문 세부 사실 3가지 이상, 인과관계, 비교 대조를 포함하고 Check & Compare로 모범 답안과 비교한 뒤 수정하세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students draft 100–140 words, run Check & Compare, check the hidden 115–130 word model, and revise (G1: follow the 5-step Paragraph Outline; G2: integrate passive voice, lists, and contrast smoothly).
teachingScript.misconception: Forgetting worker impacts, adding outside political opinions, or ending without a clear concluding sentence ("Overall,...").
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Check word count (100–140), verify "According to the article," at the start, and ensure both open vs. paused services and both worker types are covered without outside facts.
teachingScript.transition: Before submitting, complete the 6-item Self-Check carefully.

teachingScript.objective: Verify all 6 Self-Check boxes, submit with studentName and studentCode, and review the core takeaway.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Confirm every student completes Self-Check, enters Student Name and Student Code, clicks Submit lesson, and checks submission confirmation.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Check all six boxes in Self-Check / to confirm your evidence, comparison, / language, and word count. / Enter your Student Name / and Student Code accurately, / then click Submit lesson. / Great job explaining / how budgets, Congress, / and shutdowns work!
teachingScript.scriptKo: Self-Check의 6개 항목을 모두 체크해 근거, 비교, 언어 표현, 단어 수를 점검하세요. 이름(Student Name)과 학생 코드(Student Code)를 정확히 입력한 뒤 Submit lesson을 누르세요. 연방 예산, 의회, 셧다운의 작동 방식을 훌륭하게 정리했습니다!
teachingScript.studentActions: Students check all 6 Self-Check items, submit name/code/answers, and verify confirmation (G1: confirm word count and name/code fields; G2: inspect auto-graded MCQ explanations after submit).
teachingScript.misconception: Submitting without entering Student Name, Student Code, or final Writing Task text.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Verify all fields are completed before clicking Submit lesson, and confirm separate attempts appear properly in Teacher Monitor.
teachingScript.transition: In our next civics lesson, we will continue examining how public budgets affect community services.

teachersOpeningScript.label: Step 1 — Welcome & Topic Framing
teachersOpeningScript.english: Welcome to Unit 5! / Today we are reading a civics article / called "What Happens When a Government Shuts Down?" / Notice the subtitle: / "When the people in charge can’t agree, / things start to pause."
teachersOpeningScript.directKorean: Unit 5에 오신 것을 환영합니다! / 오늘 우리는 시민(Civics) 글을 읽습니다 / "What Happens When a Government Shuts Down?"이라고 불리는 / 부제목에 주목하세요: / "책임자들이 합의할 수 없을 때, / 일들이 멈추기 시작한다."

teachersOpeningScript.label: Step 2 — Three-Page Source & Neutrality Rule
teachersOpeningScript.english: Our reading comes from three classroom source images / reproduced word for word. / Remember our rule today: / stay strictly inside the article / with zero outside facts / and zero party judgment.
teachersOpeningScript.directKorean: 우리의 읽기 자료는 세 장의 교실 자료 이미지에서 왔습니다 / 단어 하나까지 그대로 옮겨진 / 오늘의 규칙을 기억하세요: / 본문 안에만 엄격하게 머무르세요 / 외부 사실은 전혀 넣지 않고 / 정당에 대한 판단도 전혀 하지 않으면서.

teachersOpeningScript.teachingPurpose: Establish strict source fidelity and political neutrality before Warm-up.

warmUpTeacherGuide.question: What important everyday services or public programs does a government provide to keep a country running and help families?
warmUpTeacherGuide.focus: Connecting everyday public infrastructure and support programs to government funding
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherTalk: Think about your daily life / from morning to night. / Roads, schools, hospitals, / emergency help after a storm—/ what services does a government provide / to keep a country running?
warmUpTeacherGuide.korean: 아침부터 밤까지의 일상을 떠올려 보세요. 도로, 학교, 병원, 폭풍 뒤의 긴급 구호 등 나라를 계속 돌아가게 하기 위해 정부가 제공하는 서비스에는 어떤 것들이 있을까요?
warmUpTeacherGuide.sampleAnswer: A government helps keep a country running by providing important services like building roads, funding schools, supporting healthcare, and offering emergency help.
likelyResponses: Schools, roads, police or military defense, and hospitals.
Programs that help older people or families who need food or disaster help.
warmUpTeacherGuide.followUp: Keep that list in mind! In Section 1, check which exact services and three special programs the article names.
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherFollowUpKorean: 그 목록을 기억해 두세요! 1단원 본문에서 글이 정확히 어떤 서비스들과 세 가지 지원 프로그램을 꼽는지 확인해 봅시다.
warmUpTeacherGuide.caution: Keep examples general; do not introduce budget numbers or outside agencies.
warmUpTeacherGuide.purpose: Prime students for Section 1 ("First, What Does the Government Do?").

warmUpTeacherGuide.question: Why might leaders in charge disagree about how to spend government money, and what problem could happen if they miss a deadline?
warmUpTeacherGuide.focus: Competing spending priorities and the consequence of missing a budget deadline
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherTalk: Imagine a group of leaders / sharing one budget. / Why might some want to spend more / on one thing, / while others want to cut or change taxes? / And what happens / if time runs out before they agree?
warmUpTeacherGuide.korean: 하나의 예산을 나누어 결정해야 하는 지도자들을 상상해 보세요. 왜 어떤 사람은 한 분야에 더 쓰자고 하고 다른 사람은 줄이거나 세금을 바꾸자고 할까요? 그리고 합의 전에 시간이 다 지나가면 어떤 문제가 생길까요?
warmUpTeacherGuide.sampleAnswer: Leaders might disagree on how to spend money because they have different priorities for schools, defense, or taxes, and missing a deadline could pause spending.
likelyResponses: Different lawmakers care about different programs or taxes.
If they miss the deadline, nobody can approve spending money.
warmUpTeacherGuide.followUp: When we read Sections 2 and 3, find the exact word for why spending stops when a deadline passes.
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherFollowUpKorean: 2단원과 3단원을 읽을 때 마감 시한이 지나면 왜 지출이 멈추는지 설명하는 핵심 단어(permission)를 찾아보세요.
warmUpTeacherGuide.caution: Keep neutrality strict; frame disagreement as differing spending choices, not party blame.
warmUpTeacherGuide.purpose: Prepare students for Sections 2 and 3 on budget permission, Congress, and deadlines.

warmUpTeacherGuide.question: If a government temporarily runs out of permission to spend money, which services do you think should stay open and which ones might pause?
warmUpTeacherGuide.focus: Distinguishing essential/mandatory continuity from non-essential pauses
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherTalk: Suppose money stops for a short time. / Should everything close at once, / or must some critical work keep going? / Which services feel essential, / and which ones could pause for a while?
warmUpTeacherGuide.korean: 잠시 동안 지출이 중단된다고 가정해 봅시다. 모든 것이 한꺼번에 닫아야 할까요, 아니면 꼭 필요한 일은 계속되어야 할까요? 어떤 서비스가 필수적이고, 어떤 것은 잠시 멈출 수 있을까요?
warmUpTeacherGuide.sampleAnswer: If money pauses, essential services such as national defense and air safety should stay open, while parks or museums might pause.
likelyResponses: Safety, military, and hospital/elderly support should stay open; parks or museums can close temporarily.
Even if workers stay on duty, getting paid on time might become a problem.
warmUpTeacherGuide.followUp: Now check Page 3 of the article to see the exact "Stays Open:" and "Gets Paused:" lists and how workers are treated.
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherFollowUpKorean: 이제 본문 3쪽에서 정확한 "계속 운영(Stays Open:)"과 "일시 중단(Gets Paused:)" 목록과 근로자 처우를 직접 확인해 봅시다.
warmUpTeacherGuide.caution: Remind students that once we read Page 3, answers must follow the article’s exact two lists.
warmUpTeacherGuide.purpose: Prepare students for Section 4’s contrast between open and paused services and worker impacts.

sourceReadingGuide.title: Source Reading & 3-Image Boundaries Guide
sourceReadingGuide.description: The canonical article is reproduced verbatim across three ordered source images without adaptation, reconstruction of cropped labels, or outside facts.
points: Outside Reading Attribution: "Source: Teacher-provided classroom source images. Article wording reproduced as supplied."

Image 1 (Page 1): Title ("What Happens When a Government Shuts Down?"), Subtitle ("When the people in charge can’t agree, things start to pause"), Section 1 ("First, What Does the Government Do?"), and Section 2 ("What Is a Government Shutdown?").

Image 2 (Page 2): Section 3 ("Why Can’t They Just Agree?"), intro paragraph, lead-in ("Sometimes they disagree on:"), 3 disagreement bullets, and closing line ("If no agreement is reached by the deadline, shutdown happens.").
Image 3 (Page 3): Section 4 ("What Happens During a Shutdown?"), intro paragraph, "Stays Open:" + 3 bullets, and "Gets Paused:" + 3 bullets ending in “furloughed” (no trailing period).

Visual-Only Rule: Any embedded or cropped text inside classroom image graphics is visual-only and is never reconstructed or added. Preserve exact curly apostrophes (’), curly quotes (“furloughed”), "Democrats and Republican lawmakers", and "shutdown happens".

detailedReadingGuide.sourceLayoutNote: Detailed guide covers all 30 canonical units with no merge and no split: Title (1), Subtitle (1), 4 Headings (4), Paragraph sentences (11), Lead-ins (3), Disagreement bullets (3), Stays Open bullets (3), Gets Paused bullets 1–2 (2), and both sentences of the final bullet (2).

sentenceAnalysis.original: What Happens When a Government Shuts Down?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: What Happens / When a Government / Shuts Down?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무슨 일이 일어나는가 / 정부가 / 문을 닫을(멈출) 때?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 정부가 셧다운(업무 정지)되면 무슨 일이 일어날까?

mustKnowChunks.use: 인과 과정이나 사건의 결과를 소개하는 설명문 제목 패턴입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: What Happens When Congress Misses a Budget Deadline?

mustKnowChunks.use: 동사구로 기관이나 서비스의 운영이 중단될 때 씁니다. (명사형은 shutdown)
mustKnowChunks.example: Some services must pause or shut down without funding.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 의문대명사 What이 주어 역할을 하며 단수 동사 Happens를 취하고, 시간 부사절 접속사 When이 이끄는 절에서 3인칭 단수 주어 a Government에 맞춰 동사 Shuts에 -s가 붙습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Think of a big machine / that runs a whole country. / Sometimes / the people who pay for the machine / stop agreeing. / This title asks / what happens to that country / when the government has to pause.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 나라 전체를 움직이는 커다란 기계를 떠올려 보세요. 가끔 그 기계에 돈을 대는 사람들이 서로 합의하지 못할 때가 있습니다. 이 제목은 정부가 멈춰야 할 때 나라에 어떤 일이 벌어지는지 묻고 있습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the two words "Shuts Down" in the title. Does it mean the country disappears forever, or that government work pauses?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 제목의 "Shuts Down"이라는 두 단어를 보세요. 나라가 영원히 사라진다는 뜻일까요, 아니면 정부 업무가 멈춘다는 뜻일까요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It means government work pauses or stops for a time.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 정부 업무가 잠시 멈추거나 중단된다는 뜻입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: When the people in charge can’t agree, things start to pause
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: When the people in charge / can’t agree, / things start to pause
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 책임을 맡은 사람들이 / 합의할 수 없을 때, / 일들이 멈추기 시작한다
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 책임자들이 합의하지 못하면 여러 일이 멈추기 시작한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 공식 직함 대신 의사결정을 담당하는 지도자·의원들을 쉽게 가리킬 때 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: The people in charge must vote on the new budget.

mustKnowChunks.meaning: 합의할 수 없다, 의견이 일치하지 않는다
mustKnowChunks.use: can’t는 cannot의 축약형으로, 합의에 이르지 못하는 상태를 나타냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: If lawmakers can’t agree, the plan cannot move forward.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 부사절(When ...) + 주절(things start to pause): 접속사 When이 조건·시점을 제시하고, 조동사 축약형 can’t(cannot) 뒤에는 동사원형 agree가 옵니다. start 뒤에는 to부정사(to pause)가 이어집니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: A country needs leaders / to decide how to spend money. / Here, "the people in charge" / means those leaders. / The word "can’t" / means they are unable to say yes together. / When they do not agree, / public services begin to stop.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 나라에는 돈을 어떻게 쓸지 결정할 지도자들이 필요합니다. 여기서 "the people in charge"는 그 지도자들을 뜻합니다. "can’t"는 함께 찬성할 수 없다는 의미이고, 그들이 합의하지 못하면 공공 서비스가 멈추기 시작합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why does the subtitle use "can’t" instead of "don’t want to"? What does "can’t agree" show?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 부제목이 왜 "don’t want to" 대신 "can’t"를 썼을까요? "can’t agree"는 무엇을 보여 주나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It shows they are unable to reach a shared agreement, so things start to pause.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 서로 공통된 합의에 도달하지 못해서 일들이 멈추기 시작한다는 점을 보여 줍니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: First, What Does the Government Do?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: First, / What Does the Government Do?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 먼저, / 정부는 무엇을 하는가?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 먼저, 정부는 어떤 일을 할까?

mustKnowChunks.use: 독자의 배경지식을 먼저 세우기 위해 첫 번째 소제목으로 자주 쓰입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: First, what does a federal budget do for public schools?

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 부사 First로 설명의 첫 단계를 열고, 일반동사 do의 의문문(What + does + 주어 + 동사원형 do?)으로 정부의 역할을 묻습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Before explaining a shutdown, / we need to know / what a government normally does. / Think of this heading / as Step 1. / It asks us / to look at everyday public services first.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 셧다운을 설명하기 전에 먼저 정부가 평소에 무슨 일을 하는지 알아야 합니다. 이 제목을 1단계라고 생각하세요. 일상적인 공공 서비스를 먼저 살펴보자고 안내하고 있습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why does the article start with "First, What Does the Government Do?" before defining a shutdown?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 글이 셧다운을 정의하기 전에 왜 "먼저, 정부는 무엇을 하는가?"로 시작할까요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Because we need to understand what services depend on government money first.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 어떤 서비스들이 정부 예산에 의존하는지 먼저 이해해야 하기 때문입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: The U.S. government provides important services that keep the country running, like defending the nation, building roads, supporting healthcare, and funding schools.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: The U.S. government provides / important services / that keep the country running, / like defending the nation, / building roads, / supporting healthcare, / and funding schools.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 미국 정부는 제공한다 / 중요한 서비스들을 / 나라가 계속 돌아가게 하는, / 국가를 방위하는 것, / 도로를 건설하는 것, / 의료를 지원하는 것, / 그리고 학교에 자금을 대는 것과 같은.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 미국 정부는 국방, 도로 건설, 의료 지원, 학교 재정 지원처럼 나라가 원활히 돌아가도록 돕는 중요한 서비스들을 제공한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: keep + 목적어 + -ing(현재분사) 형태로 어떤 대상이 계속 작동하게 두다라는 뜻입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Public funding helps keep schools and hospitals running.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: like A, B, C, and D
mustKnowChunks.meaning: A, B, C, 그리고 D와 같은
mustKnowChunks.use: 전치사 like 뒤에 동명사구(-ing) 4개를 나열하여 구체적 사례를 제시합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: The city offers services like cleaning streets, fixing bridges, and running buses.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 주격 관계대명사 that(that keep the country running)이 복수 명사 services를 수식하고, 전치사 like 뒤에 동명사 4개(defending, building, supporting, funding)가 병렬 나열되었습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Every day, / a country needs basic things / to work smoothly. / The government pays for / protection, roads, healthcare, and schools. / These four examples / are listed together / to show how wide government services are.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 매일 나라는 원활히 돌아가기 위해 기본적인 것들이 필요합니다. 정부는 국방, 도로, 의료, 학교에 비용을 댑니다. 이 네 가지 예시는 정부 서비스의 범위가 얼마나 넓은지 보여 주기 위해 나란히 제시되었습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Spot the four -ing examples after "like." Which four services keep the country running?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "like" 뒤에 나오는 네 가지 -ing 예시를 찾아보세요. 어떤 네 가지 서비스가 나라를 돌아가게 하나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Defending the nation, building roads, supporting healthcare, and funding schools.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 국가 방위, 도로 건설, 의료 지원, 그리고 학교 자금 지원입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: It also helps people through programs like Social Security, food assistance, and disaster relief.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: It also helps people / through programs / like Social Security, / food assistance, / and disaster relief.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 그것은 또한 사람들을 돕는다 / 프로그램들을 통해 / 사회보장제도, / 식량 지원, / 그리고 재난 구호와 같은.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 또한 사회보장제도, 식량 지원, 재난 구호 같은 프로그램들을 통해 국민을 돕는다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 어떤 수단이나 지원 제도를 거쳐 돕는지 밝힐 때 전치사 through를 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: The agency supports families through programs like food assistance.

mustKnowChunks.use: 자연재해나 큰 피해가 난 사람들을 돕는 공적 지원을 뜻하는 명사구입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: After the storm, disaster relief helped local communities.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 대명사 It은 앞 문장의 The U.S. government를 가리킵니다. 전치사 through가 방법을 나타내고, 전치사 like가 3개의 명사 프로그램 예시(Social Security, food assistance, disaster relief)를 연결합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: The government does not only build roads. / It also directly helps people / who need extra support. / Programs like Social Security, / food help, / and emergency disaster relief / protect citizens in daily life and crises.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 정부는 도로만 건설하는 것이 아닙니다. 추가적인 도움이 필요한 사람들도 직접 돕습니다. 사회보장제도, 식량 지원, 긴급 재난 구호 같은 프로그램들이 일상과 위기 속에서 시민들을 보호합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What does "It" refer to at the start of this sentence, and what three programs are listed?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이 문장 처음의 "It"은 무엇을 가리키며, 어떤 세 가지 프로그램이 나열되어 있나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "It" refers to the U.S. government, and the programs are Social Security, food assistance, and disaster relief.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "It"은 미국 정부를 가리키고, 프로그램은 사회보장제도, 식량 지원, 재난 구호입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: To keep all this going, the government needs money, and that money comes from something called a federal budget.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: To keep all this going, / the government needs money, / and that money comes from / something called a federal budget.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 이 모든 것을 계속 유지하기 위해, / 정부는 돈이 필요하다, / 그리고 그 돈은 ~에서 나온다 / 연방 예산이라고 불리는 것.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 이 모든 일을 계속 운영하려면 정부에 돈이 필요하며, 그 돈은 연방 예산이라는 것에서 나온다.

mustKnowChunks.meaning: 이 모든 것을 계속 운영하기 위해
mustKnowChunks.use: 문두의 to부정사(목적: ~하기 위해)로, 앞 문단 전체의 서비스를 all this로 묶어 받습니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: To keep all this going, lawmakers must approve funding.

mustKnowChunks.use: something + 과거분사(called) 구조로 낯선 핵심 용어를 자연스럽게 소개합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: That money comes from something called a federal budget.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 부사적 용법의 to부정사(To keep...)가 목적을 나타내고, 등위접속사 and가 두 절을 잇습니다. 뒷절의 called a federal budget은 앞선 something을 수식하는 과거분사구입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: All of these services / cost money every single day. / To keep roads, schools, and programs running, / the government needs a plan for cash. / That spending plan / is called a federal budget.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이 모든 서비스에는 매일 돈이 듭니다. 도로, 학교, 지원 프로그램을 계속 운영하려면 정부에 자금 계획이 필요합니다. 그 지출 계획이 바로 연방 예산이라고 불립니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at "all this." What does "all this" summarize, and where does the money come from?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "all this"를 보세요. "all this"는 무엇을 요약하며, 그 돈은 어디에서 나오나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It summarizes all the services and programs in Paragraph 1, and the money comes from a federal budget.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 1문단의 모든 서비스와 프로그램을 요약하며, 돈은 연방 예산에서 나옵니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: What Is a Government Shutdown?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: What Is / a Government Shutdown?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무엇인가 / 정부 셧다운이란?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 정부 셧다운이란 무엇일까?

mustKnowChunks.use: 핵심 개념의 정의를 제시하는 소제목 질문입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: What Is a Federal Budget?

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 의문사 What + be동사 Is + 명사구 주어(a Government Shutdown)로 이루어진 정의 질문 문장입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now that we know / what the government does / and how it pays for it, / we reach Step 2. / This heading introduces / a key civics term. / In the next two lines, / we learn the clear meaning of a government shutdown.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 정부가 무슨 일을 하고 어떻게 비용을 대는지 알았으니 2단계로 넘어갑니다. 이 제목은 중요한 시민(Civics) 용어를 소개합니다. 다음 두 문장에서 정부 셧다운의 정확한 뜻을 배우게 됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Now we move from what the government does to defining a shutdown. Read the next two sentences for the exact definition.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이제 정부가 하는 일에서 셧다운의 정의로 넘어갑니다. 정확한 정의를 찾기 위해 다음 두 문장을 읽어 봅시다.

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Let us look for when it happens and what it means for spending.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 언제 일어나는지, 그리고 지출에 어떤 의미가 있는지 찾아보겠습니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: A government shutdown happens when Congress can’t agree on a new budget before a deadline.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: A government shutdown happens / when Congress can’t agree / on a new budget / before a deadline.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 정부 셧다운은 일어난다 / 의회가 합의할 수 없을 때 / 새로운 예산에 대해 / 마감 시한 전에.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 정부 셧다운은 의회가 마감 시한 전까지 새 예산에 합의하지 못할 때 발생한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 무엇에 대해 의견을 모으는지 말할 때 동사 agree 뒤에 전치사 on을 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Congress has to agree on a new budget every year.

mustKnowChunks.use: 반드시 지켜야 하는 최종 기한을 앞둘 때 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Lawmakers must vote before a deadline.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 단수 주어(A government shutdown)에 현재시제 동사 happens가 쓰여 일반적 원리/정의를 설명합니다. 시간·조건 접속사 when이 이끄는 절에서 can’t(cannot)는 합의 불가 상태를 나타냅니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Think of a due date / for paying a bill or signing a permission slip. / Congress has a deadline / to agree on a new spending plan. / When they cannot agree in time, / a shutdown begins.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 고지서를 내거나 동의서에 서명해야 하는 마감일을 떠올려 보세요. 의회에는 새 지출 계획에 합의해야 하는 마감 시한이 있습니다. 제때 합의하지 못하면 셧다운이 시작됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What are the two conditions needed for a shutdown here? Look at "Congress" and "deadline."
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 여기서 셧다운이 일어나기 위한 두 가지 요소는 무엇인가요? "Congress"와 "deadline"을 보세요.

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Congress cannot agree on a new budget, and they miss the deadline.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 의회가 새 예산에 합의하지 못하고, 마감 시한을 넘기는 것입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: That means the government doesn’t have permission to spend money, so many services must pause or shut down.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: That means / the government doesn’t have permission / to spend money, / so many services must pause or shut down.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 그것은 의미한다 / 정부가 허가를 가지고 있지 않다는 것을 / 돈을 쓸, / 그래서 많은 서비스들이 멈추거나 문을 닫아야 한다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 그것은 정부가 돈을 쓸 권한(허가)이 없다는 뜻이므로, 많은 서비스가 일시 중단되거나 문을 닫아야 한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 법적으로 예산을 집행할 수 있는 승인 상태를 뜻하며, 부정문(doesn’t have permission)으로 지출 불가를 설명합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Without a budget, the agency doesn’t have permission to spend money.

mustKnowChunks.use: 조동사 must는 선택이 아니라 법적·재정적 필연(반드시 ~해야 함)을 나타냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Non-essential offices must pause or shut down until funding returns.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: That means (that) ... 구문에서 명사 permission을 to부정사(to spend money)가 수식합니다. 등위접속사 so가 인과 결과("그래서")를 연결하며, 조동사 must가 필연적 의무를 나타냅니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Even if the country has money, / the government cannot spend it / without permission. / Permission here means legal approval / from the budget vote. / Because there is no permission, / many services must stop for a while.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 나라에 돈이 있더라도 허가(승인)가 없으면 정부는 돈을 쓸 수 없습니다. 여기서 permission은 예산 투표를 통한 법적 승인을 뜻합니다. 허가가 없기 때문에 많은 서비스가 잠시 멈춰야만 합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Notice the words "permission" and "must." Why can’t the government just spend money anyway?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "permission"과 "must"라는 단어에 주목하세요. 왜 정부는 그냥 돈을 쓰지 못할까요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Because it doesn’t have permission without an approved budget, so many services must pause or shut down.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 승인된 예산 없이는 지출 허가가 없기 때문에, 많은 서비스가 멈추거나 중단되어야 합니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Why Can’t They Just Agree?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Why Can’t They / Just Agree?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 왜 그들은 ~할 수 없는가 / 그냥 합의하는 것을?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 그들은 왜 그냥 합의하지 못할까?

mustKnowChunks.use: 독자가 흔히 품는 자연스러운 의문을 그대로 제목에 담아 이유 설명을 여는 구어체적 질문입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Why can’t lawmakers just agree before the deadline?

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 의문부사 Why + 부정 조동사 축약형 can’t + 주어 they + 부사 just + 동사원형 agree로, 합의가 어려운 이유를 묻는 의문문입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: You might wonder / why leaders do not simply shake hands / and pass the budget quickly. / The word "just" / shows that it sounds easy from the outside. / This section explains / why reaching an agreement is actually hard.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 여러분은 지도자들이 왜 그냥 악수하고 예산을 빨리 통과시키지 않는지 궁금할 수 있습니다. "just"라는 단어는 밖에서 보기에 쉬워 보인다는 느낌을 줍니다. 이 부분은 왜 합의에 이르기가 실제로 어려운지 설명합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Who does "They" refer to in "Why Can’t They Just Agree?"
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "Why Can’t They Just Agree?"에서 "They"는 누구를 가리키나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: The people in Congress who have to agree on the budget.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 예산에 합의해야 하는 의회의 사람들입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: U.S. Congress is made up of two groups: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: U.S. Congress / is made up of / two groups: / the House of Representatives / and the Senate.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 미국 의회는 / ~로 구성되어 있다 / 두 집단으로: / 하원 / 그리고 상원.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 미국 의회는 하원과 상원이라는 두 집단으로 구성되어 있다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 어떤 조직이나 전체가 어떤 부분들로 이루어졌는지 설명할 때 쓰는 수동형 숙어입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: The committee is made up of members from both groups.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: the House of Representatives and the Senate
mustKnowChunks.use: 미국 의회(U.S. Congress)를 이루는 두 입법 기관의 고유 명칭입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Both the House of Representatives and the Senate vote on the budget.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 수동형 구동사 is made up of(~로 구성되다) 뒤에 콜론(:)이 와서 two groups의 구체적 이름(the House of Representatives and the Senate)을 바로 밝혀 줍니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: U.S. Congress is not just one single room / of people. / Instead, / it is built from two separate groups. / One group is the House of Representatives, / and the other group is the Senate.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 미국 의회는 사람들이 모인 하나의 방이 아닙니다. 대신 두 개의 별도 집단으로 이루어져 있습니다. 한 집단은 하원이고, 다른 한 집단은 상원입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Notice the phrase "is made up of." What are the two parts that make up U.S. Congress?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "is made up of"라는 표현을 보세요. 미국 의회를 이루는 두 부분은 무엇인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: The House of Representatives and the Senate.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 하원과 상원입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: They have to vote to approve the budget, and if they (usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers) disagree about how to spend the money, the government can’t move forward.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: They have to vote / to approve the budget, / and if they (usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers) disagree / about how to spend the money, / the government can’t move forward.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 그들은 투표해야 한다 / 예산을 승인하기 위해, / 그리고 만약 그들이 (보통 민주당과 공화당 의원들) 의견이 다르면 / 그 돈을 어떻게 쓸지에 대해, / 정부는 앞으로 나아갈 수 없다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 이들은 예산을 승인하기 위해 투표를 해야 하며, 만약 의원들(보통 민주당과 공화당 의원들)이 예산 지출 방식에 대해 의견을 달리하면 정부는 앞으로 나아갈 수 없다.

mustKnowChunks.use: have to(의무) + vote + to부정사(목적)로 의회의 공식 절차를 표현합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Lawmakers have to vote to approve the new spending plan.

mustKnowChunks.use: 일이나 정부가 막히지 않고 계속 진행되는 상태를 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Without approval, the government can’t move forward.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 괄호 (usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers)는 주어 they가 구체적으로 누구인지 보충 설명합니다. 조건 접속사 if 절(if they ... disagree)이 현재시제로 쓰여 주절(the government can’t move forward)의 조건을 제시하며, how to spend(의문사 + to부정사)가 about의 목적어 역할을 합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Both groups in Congress / must vote yes / to approve the money plan. / The words inside parentheses / tell us who "they" usually are: / Democrats and Republican lawmakers. / If those lawmakers disagree / on how to spend money, / the government gets stuck.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 의회의 두 집단 모두 예산 계획을 승인하려면 찬성 투표를 해야 합니다. 괄호 안의 말은 그들이 보통 누구인지, 즉 민주당과 공화당 의원들이라고 알려 줍니다. 만약 그 의원들이 돈 쓰는 방법에 동의하지 못하면 정부는 멈춰 서게 됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why did the writer put "(usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers)" in parentheses, and what does the "if" clause tell us?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 글쓴이는 왜 "(usually Democrats and Republican lawmakers)"를 괄호에 넣었으며, "if" 절은 무엇을 알려 주나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: The parentheses clarify who "they" are, and the "if" clause shows that disagreement stops the government from moving forward.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 괄호는 "they"가 누구인지 명확히 해 주고, "if" 절은 의견 불일치가 정부의 진행을 막는 조건임을 보여 줍니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Sometimes they disagree on:
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Sometimes / they disagree on:
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 때때로 / 그들은 다음에 대해 의견이 다르다:
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 그들이 의견 차이를 보이는 대표적인 내용은 다음과 같다:

mustKnowChunks.use: 뒤에 이어지는 글머리 기호(bullet list) 항목들을 이끄는 도입문(lead-in)입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Lawmakers often disagree on how to spend public money.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 빈도 부사 Sometimes + 동사 disagree + 전치사 on + 콜론(:)으로, 구체적인 갈등 항목 3가지를 나열할 준비를 합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: People do not disagree / about nothing. / There are specific money questions / that cause arguments in Congress. / This short line introduces / a three-point list of those disagreements.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 사람들은 아무 이유 없이 의견이 다른 것이 아닙니다. 의회에서 논쟁을 일으키는 구체적인 예산 문제들이 있습니다. 이 짧은 문장은 그 불일치 사항 세 가지 목록을 안내합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the colon at the end of "Sometimes they disagree on:". What should we expect right after a colon?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "Sometimes they disagree on:" 끝의 콜론(:)을 보세요. 콜론 바로 뒤에 무엇이 나올 것으로 예상할 수 있나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: A list of examples showing what lawmakers disagree about.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 의원들이 무엇에 대해 의견이 다른지 보여 주는 예시 목록이 나옵니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: How much to spend on defense or schools
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: How much to spend / on defense or schools
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 얼마나 쓸지 / 국방이나 학교에
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 국방이나 학교에 얼마를 지출할지

mustKnowChunks.use: 의문사구(How much) + to부정사(to spend) 형태로 지출 규모에 대한 쟁점을 간결히 적습니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Lawmakers debate how much to spend on defense or schools.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 명사구 형태(How much + to부정사)로 쓰인 목록 항목이며, 전치사 on이 지출 대상(defense or schools)을 연결합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Budget money is limited. / One big question is / how much money should go to defense / compared to schools. / Different lawmakers / want different amounts for each.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 예산으로 쓸 수 있는 돈은 정해져 있습니다. 큰 질문 중 하나는 학교에 비해 국방에 얼마나 많은 돈을 배정할지입니다. 의원마다 각 분야에 원하는 금액이 다릅니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: In this first bullet, what two areas are compared for spending?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이 첫 번째 목록에서 지출을 두고 어떤 두 분야가 언급되나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Defense or schools.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 국방이나 학교입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Whether to cut or increase certain programs
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Whether to cut or increase / certain programs
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 줄일지 혹은 늘릴지 / 특정 프로그램들을
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 특정 프로그램 예산을 삭감할지 증액할지

mustKnowChunks.use: Whether + to부정사로 상반된 두 선택지(cut vs. increase) 사이의 갈등을 나타냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Congress must decide whether to cut or increase certain programs.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 접속사 Whether + to부정사(to cut or increase)가 대조 동사 쌍(cut vs. increase)을 연결해 목적어 certain programs를 취합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Another question is / whether a program should get less money / or more money. / "Cut" means reducing funding, / while "increase" means raising it. / Lawmakers often disagree on this choice.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 또 다른 질문은 특정 프로그램이 돈을 더 적게 받아야 하는지 더 많이 받아야 하는지입니다. "cut"은 예산을 줄이는 것이고, "increase"는 늘리는 것입니다. 의원들은 이 선택을 두고 자주 이견을 보입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the contrast inside this bullet. Which two opposite verbs does "Whether to" connect?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이 목록 안의 대조를 보세요. "Whether to"는 어떤 두 반대 동사를 연결하나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "Cut" and "increase."
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "cut(줄이다)"과 "increase(늘리다)"입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Tax changes or debt limits
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Tax changes / or debt limits
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 세금 변경 / 또는 부채 한도
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 세금 변화 또는 부채 한도

mustKnowChunks.use: 예산 협상에서 논쟁이 되는 두 가지 재정 쟁점을 명사구로 압축해 제시합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Disagreements can involve tax changes or debt limits.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 앞의 두 불릿(의문사+to부정사)과 달리 세 번째 불릿은 간결한 복수 명사구 병렬(Tax changes or debt limits)로 되어 있습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Money plans also involve / how much tax people pay / and how much money the government can borrow. / "Tax changes" means changing taxes. / "Debt limits" means setting a top limit / on borrowing.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 예산 계획에는 사람들이 내는 세금과 정부가 빌릴 수 있는 금액도 포함됩니다. "Tax changes"는 세금을 바꾸는 것이고, "debt limits"는 돈을 빌릴 수 있는 최대 한도를 정하는 것입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What are the third type of items lawmakers may disagree on, besides spending and programs?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 지출 규모와 프로그램 외에 의원들이 의견이 다를 수 있는 세 번째 항목은 무엇인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Tax changes or debt limits.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 세금 변경이나 부채 한도입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: If no agreement is reached by the deadline, shutdown happens.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: If no agreement is reached / by the deadline, / shutdown happens.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 만약 아무 합의도 도달되지 않으면 / 마감 시한까지, / 셧다운이 일어난다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 마감 시한까지 합의에 이르지 못하면 셧다운이 일어난다.

mustKnowChunks.use: reach an agreement(합의에 도달하다)의 수동태 부정(no agreement is reached)으로, 결과 중심의 공식 문체입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: If no agreement is reached, public services must pause.

mustKnowChunks.use: 전치사 by는 완료 시점("~까지")을 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Lawmakers must vote by the deadline.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 조건절 If + 현재 수동태(is reached) + 완료 기한 전치사구(by the deadline), 주절(shutdown happens): 여기서 shutdown은 관사 없이 현상 전체를 가리키는 불가산 개념처럼 쓰였습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: The clock keeps ticking / toward the final due date. / "Is reached" is passive / because we focus on the agreement itself, / not one person. / If the deadline arrives with no deal, / shutdown happens.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 시계는 최종 마감일을 향해 계속 움직입니다. "is reached"는 특정 개인이 아니라 합의 그 자체에 초점을 맞추기 때문에 수동태입니다. 합의 없이 마감 시한이 오면 셧다운이 일어납니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the passive verb "is reached" and the exact closing words "shutdown happens." What must happen by the deadline to stop a shutdown?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 수동태 "is reached"와 끝맺음 말 "shutdown happens"를 보세요. 셧다운을 막으려면 마감 시한까지 무엇이 이루어져야 하나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: An agreement must be reached by the deadline.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 마감 시한까지 합의가 이루어져야 합니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: What Happens During a Shutdown?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: What Happens / During a Shutdown?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무슨 일이 일어나는가 / 셧다운 동안에?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 셧다운 기간 동안에는 무슨 일이 일어날까?

mustKnowChunks.use: 특정 기간이나 사건이 이어지는 동안을 나타낼 때 전치사 during + 명사를 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Some services stay open during a shutdown.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 의문사 What(주어) + 동사 Happens + 기간 전치사구 During a Shutdown으로, 마지막 핵심 내용을 안내하는 소제목입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now we know why a shutdown starts. / Next, we ask / what real life looks like / while the shutdown is happening. / This final section compares / what stays open and what pauses.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 셧다운이 왜 시작되는지 알았습니다. 다음으로 셧다운이 진행되는 동안 실제 상황이 어떤지 살펴봅니다. 이 마지막 부분은 계속 열리는 것과 멈추는 것을 비교합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Does "During a Shutdown" mean before it starts, or while it is taking place?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "During a Shutdown"은 시작되기 전을 뜻하나요, 아니면 진행되는 동안을 뜻하나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: While the shutdown is taking place.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 셧다운이 진행되는 동안을 뜻합니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: When the government shuts down, some things stop and some keep going.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: When the government shuts down, / some things stop / and some keep going.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 정부가 문을 닫을(멈출) 때, / 어떤 것들은 멈추고 / 그리고 어떤 것들은 계속 진행된다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 정부가 셧다운되면 어떤 일들은 멈추고 어떤 일들은 계속 유지된다.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: some things stop and some keep going
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 어떤 것들은 멈추고 어떤 것들은 계속 이어진다
mustKnowChunks.use: some ~ and some ... 구조로 대조적인 두 결과를 한 문장에 깔끔히 담습니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: When funding pauses, some offices close and some keep going.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 시간/조건 부사절(When ...) 뒤에 주절이 some things stop(멈추다)과 some keep going(계속되다)을 접속사 and로 대조 연결합니다. keep + -ing는 계속 진행을 나타냅니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: A government shutdown / does not mean / every single building locks its doors. / Instead, / the government splits into two paths. / Some services stop right away, / while other important ones keep running.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 정부 셧다운이 모든 건물의 문을 다 잠근다는 뜻은 아닙니다. 대신 정부의 일이 두 갈래로 나뉩니다. 어떤 서비스는 멈추고, 다른 중요한 서비스들은 계속 돌아갑니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: True or false based on this sentence: Everything in the U.S. government stops completely during a shutdown.
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이 문장에 근거해 맞는지 틀리는지 답해 보세요. 셧다운 동안 미국 정부의 모든 것이 완전히 멈춘다.

teachingTranscript.english: Student: False! Some things stop, and some keep going.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 틀렸습니다! 어떤 것들은 멈추고 어떤 것들은 계속 이어집니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Some workers still have to work but don’t get paid until later.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Some workers / still have to work / but don’t get paid / until later.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 일부 노동자들은 / 여전히 일해야 한다 / 하지만 급여를 받지 못한다 / 나중이 될 때까지는.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 일부 근로자들은 여전히 일해야 하지만 나중까지 급여를 받지 못한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: have to + 동사원형으로 의무적으로 계속 출근해야 함을 나타냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Essential workers still have to work during a shutdown.

mustKnowChunks.meaning: 나중이 될 때까지 돈을 받지 못한다
mustKnowChunks.use: get + 과거분사(get paid: 급여를 받다)의 부정문과 until later가 결합해 지급 지연을 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: They work every day, even though they don’t get paid until later.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 등위접속사 but이 의무(still have to work)와 급여 지연(don’t get paid until later)을 강하게 대조합니다. get paid는 수동 의미의 표현이고 don’t는 do not의 축약형입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Even when a service stays open, / the paychecks might wait. / Some employees must keep doing their jobs / every day. / However, / they do not receive their pay / until the budget problem ends later.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 서비스가 계속 열려 있더라도 월급 지급은 미루어질 수 있습니다. 일부 직원들은 매일 자기 일을 계속해야만 합니다. 하지만 예산 문제가 나중에 해결될 때까지는 급여를 받지 못합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the contrast word "but." What is unfair or difficult about what happens to these workers?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 대조를 나타내는 "but"을 보세요. 이 근로자들에게 일어나는 일 중 무엇이 힘들고 부담스러울까요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: They still have to work, but they don’t get paid until later.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 여전히 일은 해야 하지만, 나중까지 급여를 받지 못합니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: This can be really hard for families who depend on those jobs.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: This can be really hard / for families / who depend on those jobs.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 이것은 정말 힘들 수 있다 / 가족들에게 / 그 일자리들에 의존하는.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 이는 그 일자리에 생계를 의존하는 가족들에게 매우 힘든 일이 될 수 있다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 생활비나 생계를 특정 수입원에 기대어 살아갈 때 depend on을 씁니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Many families depend on those jobs for food and rent.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 지시대명사 This는 앞 문장(일하면서도 급여를 늦게 받는 상황) 전체를 가리킵니다. 주격 관계대명사 who가 복수 명사 families를 수식해 depend on those jobs를 연결합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Missing a paycheck / is not just a number on paper. / Families need regular pay / for daily life. / So waiting to be paid / can create real stress for households / that rely on those government jobs.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 월급이 제때 나오지 않는 것은 서류상의 숫자 문제가 아닙니다. 가족들은 일상생활을 위해 정기적인 급여가 필요합니다. 그래서 급여를 기다리는 것은 그 정부 일자리에 의존하는 가정에 큰 어려움이 될 수 있습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What does "This" refer to, and who is affected according to this sentence?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 여기서 "This"는 무엇을 가리키며, 이 문장에 따르면 누가 영향을 받나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "This" refers to working without getting paid until later, and it affects families who depend on those jobs.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "This"는 일하면서도 나중까지 급여를 받지 못하는 상황을 가리키며, 그 일자리에 의존하는 가족들이 영향을 받습니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Stays Open:
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Stays / Open:
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 계속 열리는 것:
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 계속 운영되는 분야:

mustKnowChunks.use: 셧다운 중에도 중단되지 않고 계속 운영되는 항목들의 소제목(범주 표지)입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Stays Open: essential safety and mail services.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 2형식 동사 stay + 형용사 open(열린 상태를 유지하다)이 3인칭 단수형(Stays Open:)으로 쓰여 아래 3개 목록의 공통 제목 역할을 합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now the article / sorts government work into two clear lists. / The first list / is labeled "Stays Open:". / Everything in this group / keeps operating during a shutdown.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 글은 정부 업무를 두 개의 분명한 목록으로 나눕니다. 첫 번째 목록의 제목은 "계속 운영되는 분야:"입니다. 이 묶음에 들어가는 모든 것은 셧다운 중에도 계속 운영됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why does the author group the next items under "Stays Open:" and "Gets Paused:"?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 글쓴이는 왜 다음 항목들을 "Stays Open:"과 "Gets Paused:"로 나누어 묶었을까요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: To make it easy to compare what continues and what stops during a shutdown.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 셧다운 동안 계속되는 것과 멈추는 것을 쉽게 비교할 수 있도록 하기 위해서입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Military and national security (but workers may not be paid right away)
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Military and national security / (but workers may not be paid right away)
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 군사 및 국가 안보 / (하지만 근로자들은 즉시 급여를 받지 못할 수 있다)
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 군사 및 국가 안보 (단, 근로자들은 바로 급여를 받지 못할 수 있음)

mustKnowChunks.use: 나라를 지키는 핵심 방위 영역을 묶어 부르는 표현입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Military and national security stay open during a shutdown.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: may not be paid right away
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 즉시 급여를 받지 못할 수 있다
mustKnowChunks.use: 조동사 may(가능성) + 부정(not) + 수동태(be paid)로 급여 지급이 늦어질 가능성을 나타냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Service members work, though they may not be paid right away.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 괄호 안의 절이 접속사 but으로 대조를 추가하고, 조동사 부정 수동태(may not be paid)와 시간 부사구 right away(즉시)가 함께 쓰였습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Protecting the country / cannot stop for a budget argument. / So military and security work / stays open. / However, / the note inside parentheses warns / that those workers might wait for their pay.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 나라를 지키는 일은 예산 다툼 때문에 멈출 수 없습니다. 그래서 군사와 국가 안보 업무는 계속 열려 있습니다. 하지만 괄호 안의 설명은 그 근로자들이 급여를 바로 받지 못할 수도 있다고 덧붙입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Even though military and national security stay open, what does the note in parentheses tell us?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 군사와 국가 안보가 계속 유지되더라도, 괄호 안의 내용은 무엇을 알려 주나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Workers may not be paid right away.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 근로자들이 즉시 급여를 받지 못할 수도 있다는 점입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Air traffic control and mail delivery
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Air traffic control / and mail delivery
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 항공 교통 관제 / 그리고 우편 배달
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 항공 교통 관제 및 우편 배달

mustKnowChunks.chunk: Air traffic control and mail delivery
mustKnowChunks.use: 비행기 안전 운항 관리와 우편물 전달이라는 일상 핵심 인프라를 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Air traffic control and mail delivery keep operating during a shutdown.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 명사구 두 개(Air traffic control, mail delivery)를 등위접속사 and로 대등하게 연결한 목록 항목입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Airplanes in the sky / still need guidance / so flights stay safe. / Letters and packages / also keep moving to homes. / Both air traffic control and mail delivery / stay open.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 하늘을 나는 비행기는 안전한 운항을 위해 여전히 안내가 필요합니다. 편지와 소포 역시 가정으로 계속 배달됩니다. 항공 교통 관제와 우편 배달 모두 계속 운영됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Which two transportation and communication services are listed in this second bullet under Stays Open?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: Stays Open의 두 번째 목록에 제시된 두 가지 교통 및 전달 서비스는 무엇인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Air traffic control and mail delivery.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 항공 교통 관제와 우편 배달입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Social Security and Medicare payments (they’re mandatory programs)
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Social Security and Medicare payments / (they’re mandatory programs)
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 사회보장 및 메디케어 지급금 / (그것들은 의무적인 프로그램들이다)
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 사회보장 및 메디케어 지급금 (의무 지출 프로그램이기 때문)

mustKnowChunks.use: 노후·의료 등을 지원하는 핵심 사회 안전망 급여를 가리킵니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Social Security and Medicare payments continue during a shutdown.

mustKnowChunks.use: they’re는 they are의 축약형이며, mandatory는 매년 새 투표 없이도 반드시 집행해야 하는 의무 성격을 뜻합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Because they’re mandatory programs, payments stay open.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 괄호 (they’re mandatory programs)가 앞의 지급금이 왜 계속되는지 이유를 보충합니다. they’re는 they are의 축약형이고 형용사 mandatory가 명사 programs를 수식합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Social Security and Medicare / send important payments to people. / The parentheses say / "they’re mandatory programs." / "Mandatory" means required by rule, / so these payments keep going even during a shutdown.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 사회보장제도와 메디케어는 사람들에게 중요한 지원금을 지급합니다. 괄호 안에는 "그것들은 의무 프로그램이다"라고 적혀 있습니다. "mandatory"는 규정에 의해 반드시 해야 한다는 뜻이므로, 셧다운 중에도 이 지급은 계속됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the word "mandatory" inside the parentheses "(they’re mandatory programs)." Why do these payments stay open?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 괄호 "(they’re mandatory programs)" 안의 "mandatory"라는 단어를 보세요. 왜 이 지급금들은 계속 유지되나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Because they are mandatory programs—they are required to continue.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 의무적인 프로그램이라서 반드시 계속되어야 하기 때문입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Gets Paused:
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Gets / Paused:
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 일시 중단되는 것:
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 일시 중단되는 분야:

mustKnowChunks.use: get + 과거분사(paused)로 외부 예산 중단으로 인해 멈추게 되는 대상 목록을 여는 표지입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Gets Paused: national parks, museums, and some inspections.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: get + 과거분사(Gets Paused) 형태의 수동 표현이 3인칭 단수 표제로 쓰여 앞선 "Stays Open:"과 형태상 대칭과 의미상 대조를 이룹니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now we look at / the second list: / "Gets Paused:". / Unlike the first group, / the items here can stop / while Congress argues over the budget. / Look closely at the next three bullets / to see what pauses.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 두 번째 목록인 "일시 중단되는 분야:"를 봅니다. 첫 번째 묶음과 달리, 여기에 나오는 항목들은 의회가 예산안을 두고 다투는 동안 멈출 수 있습니다. 무엇이 멈추는지 다음 세 항목을 자세히 살펴보세요.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Compare "Stays Open:" and "Gets Paused:". What contrast do these two headings set up?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "Stays Open:"과 "Gets Paused:"를 비교해 보세요. 이 두 소제목은 어떤 대조를 만들어 주나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Services that keep running versus services and workers that are paused.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 계속 운영되는 서비스와 일시 중단되는 서비스 및 근로자의 대조를 보여 줍니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: National parks and museums may close
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: National parks and museums / may close
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 국립공원들과 박물관들은 / 문을 닫을 수 있다
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 국립공원과 박물관이 문을 닫을 수 있다

mustKnowChunks.use: 조동사 may는 가능성이 있음을 조심스럽게 표현합니다 (무조건 전부 닫는다고 단정하지 않음).
mustKnowChunks.example: Some national parks and museums may close during a shutdown.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 복수 주어(National parks and museums) + 추측/가능 조동사 may + 동사원형 close 구조입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Public places people visit / like national parks and museums / do not always stay open. / The word "may" / tells us closing is possible, / depending on the shutdown. / They are not treated like mandatory services.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 사람들이 방문하는 국립공원이나 박물관 같은 공공장소는 항상 열려 있는 것이 아닙니다. "may"라는 단어는 셧다운 상황에 따라 문을 닫을 수 있음을 알려 줍니다. 이들은 의무적인 필수 서비스로 취급되지 않기 때문입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Notice the modal "may" in "may close." Does it say they always close, or that closing is possible?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "may close"의 조동사 "may"를 보세요. 항상 닫는다는 뜻인가요, 닫을 가능성이 있다는 뜻인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It means closing is possible.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 닫을 가능성이 있다는 뜻입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: NASA, science labs, and safety inspections may pause
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: NASA, science labs, / and safety inspections / may pause
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: NASA, 과학 연구실들, / 그리고 안전 점검들이 / 일시 멈출 수 있다
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: NASA, 과학 연구실, 그리고 안전 점검이 중단될 수 있다

mustKnowChunks.meaning: 안전 점검이 일시 중단될 수 있다
mustKnowChunks.use: 조동사 may + pause로 연구·점검 활동이 멈출 수 있음을 나타냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Science labs and safety inspections may pause until funding is approved.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 세 개의 명사구(NASA, science labs, safety inspections)가 나열 주어를 이루고 조동사 may + 동사원형 pause가 이어집니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Research and checking work / can also slow down or stop. / Space work at NASA, / science labs, / and safety checks / may pause until money is approved again. / So scientific and inspection work waits for a new budget.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 연구와 점검 업무 역시 느려지거나 멈출 수 있습니다. NASA의 우주 업무, 과학 연구실, 안전 점검은 예산이 다시 승인될 때까지 일시 중단될 수 있습니다. 따라서 과학 연구와 안전 점검 업무는 새 예산을 기다리게 됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Which three areas may pause in this second bullet under Gets Paused?
